sentences.text: Liaodactylus possessed a large and slender head measuring 13.3 cm in cranial length and 11.7 cm in mandibular length.
The jugal bone was bent slightly to create a curved margin below the eye socket and was notably narrow compared to other ctenochasmatids.
The top of the braincase consisted of fused frontal and parietal bones that curved sharply downward at the back, giving the skull a rounded rear appearance.
At the skull's rear, the basisphenoid was a short, wide, plate-like bone featuring a wide U-shaped notch at its front end.
This creature holds the distinction of being the oldest known ctenochasmatid and the first filter-feeding pterosaur discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation.
Its species name, primus, is derived from Latin, signifying that Liaodactylus is older than other members of its family.
The genus Liaodactylus was formally described by Zhou and colleagues in 2017.
The name combines "Liao," a shortened form of Liaoning, with the Greek word dactylos, meaning "finger."
Only a single specimen is known, the holotype cataloged as PMOL-AP00031 and housed at the Palaeontological Museum of Liaoning.
This fossil was unearthed from outcrops located approximately 500 meters west of Daxishan village in Jianchang, Liaoning, China.
Liaodactylus was a filter-feeder equipped with approximately 150 long, comb-like teeth arranged very closely together.
Its jaws contained about 152 needle-shaped teeth that were densely grouped and projected outward.
The first tooth in each jaw was roughly half the length of the second tooth.
When the jaws were closed, these interlocking teeth formed a comb-like structure ideal for filter-feeding.
This animal represents the first filter-feeding pterosaur found within the Yanliao biota.
The atlas and axis vertebrae were fused together, although a visible suture line remained.
Liaodactylus is classified as a filter-feeding ctenochasmatid pterosaur from the Jurassic of China.
Zhou and colleagues assigned the species to the family Ctenochasmatidae in 2017 using phylogenetic analysis.
Phylogenetic analysis places Liaodactylus closest to Ctenochasma, sharing similar jaw-to-skull ratios and outward-angled teeth.
Liaodactylus lived during the Oxfordian stage of the Late Jurassic, approximately 161.8 to 159.5 million years ago.
It inhabited a forested woodland environment containing conifers, cycads, and ferns.
The climate was cool, temperate, wet, and seasonal, with a mean temperature below 15 °C.
Fossils are known from the Tiaojishan Formation, which along with the older Haifanggou Formation forms the Yanliao biota.
A 2023 study proposed that the Liaodactylus fossils belong to the Haifanggou Formation rather than the Tiaojishan Formation.
